idiom_name: ownership-carrying return type or release guard plus one owner-side release policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: before writing the hand-over, name the owner and decide whether the receiver hands the resource back (return to pool/manager) or destroys it (delete/close), then make the safe path the only path. Where the language has a wrapper that runs code on scope exit - smart pointer, IDisposable, context manager, defer, drop guard - return the wrapper instead of the raw handle and let its deleter/release call the owner's check-in; where it does not, return a small handle whose one documented release function is the hand-back, and keep the bare destroy operation out of the client's reach. Never mix the two: a client that can choose between 'release back' and 'destroy' will eventually choose wrong, and the owner must be able to observe every return (accounting, reset-on-return, quota).
code_sketch:
resource = owner.acquire(spec)                  # owner keeps the ownership
return Handle(resource, on_exit=owner.release)  # wrapper carries the contract
...
h = factory(spec)         # client cannot leak it or destroy it by mistake
use(h)                    # scope exit => owner.release(resource)
pitfalls: A handle whose release calls destroy turns a borrowed resource into a freed one; the owner's next hand-out then observes corrupted state.
Two release paths - a documented release() plus a raw destroy the client can still reach - make wrong-way release a matter of luck instead of design.
Clients that keep the raw resource (or a borrowed reference to it) after the wrapper leaves scope defeat the hand-back silently; the wrapper must own the only reference the client receives.
Wrong move: call destroy/free on a borrowed pool item -> the pool may reissue a freed or still-tracked resource -> instead expose only the owner-bound return/check-in operation.
Wrong move: unwrap or publish the raw handle beside the return wrapper -> callers can outlive the guard and bypass reset/accounting -> instead keep the wrapper as the only public capability.

Wrong move: return shared ownership by default to make every caller convenient -> aliases obscure the final release and can keep scarce resources checked out -> instead return exclusive ownership or a scoped loan unless sharing is required.
